passages.t: A man of God at the altar of Bethel
passages.happening:
As Jeroboam stands by his altar at Bethel to burn incense, ‘there came a man of God from Judah to Bethel by the word of the LORD’ (verse 1). He cries out against the altar that a son named Josiah will be born to the house of David and will burn on it the priests of the high places and human bones (verse 2). He gives a sign: the altar will split and its ashes pour out (verse 3).

Jeroboam stretches out his hand and orders his men to seize him. The hand withers, so that he cannot pull it back, and the altar splits and its ashes pour out, as the man of God had said (verses 4-5). The king asks him to pray for him, and when he does, the king's hand is restored (verse 6).

Jeroboam invites him home to eat and offers him a reward. The man of God refuses. He would not go with him for half his possessions, he says, because the LORD commanded him not to eat bread or drink water there, nor go back by the way he came (verses 8-9). ‘So the man of God went another way and did not return by the way he had come to Bethel’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Jeroboam has just built his own altar at Bethel (12:32-33). Before the incense has finished burning, God answers with a word from Judah, from the south, where the house of David and the temple remain.

The oracle reaches about three centuries ahead to King Josiah, who reigned in Judah from about 640 to 609 BC. Second Kings tells how he tore down the Bethel altar, burned bones from the tombs on it, and left the bones of the man of God undisturbed. Readers take the naming of Josiah in different ways. Traditional interpreters take it as true prediction, one of a handful in which a future ruler is named; Cyrus in Isaiah is another. Many critical scholars think the name was added or sharpened when the history was put together in or after Josiah's day. Both agree that Kings presents the Bethel altar as condemned from the day it was founded.

In the ancient world, sharing a meal made a bond of fellowship and obligation. The command not to eat or drink in Bethel was an acted sign: God's messenger was to have no fellowship with a place under judgment, and not even to go back by the same road. The king's offer of a meal and a gift was an attempt to bring the prophet under the king's favor and so blunt his word.
passages.later: Second Kings tells what came of it. When Josiah saw the tomb, the men of the city told him, “It is the tomb of the man of God who came from Judah and pronounced these things that you have done to the altar of Bethel” (2 Kings 23:17). Isaiah names a coming king too, Cyrus (Isaiah 44:28).
passages.asks: The man of God turned down a king's table and a king's reward. Ask what favor or comfort might blunt the truth you have been given to speak. And ask whether you, like Jeroboam, want God's help without wanting God's word.

passages.t: An old prophet's lie, and a lion on the road
passages.happening:
An old prophet living in Bethel hears from his sons what the man of God did. He saddles his donkey, finds him sitting under an oak, and invites him home to eat (verses 11-15). The man of God repeats his command: he must not eat bread or drink water there (verses 16-17). Then the old prophet says, “I too am a prophet like you” (verse 18), and claims that an angel told him to bring the man home to eat. ‘The old prophet was lying to him’ (verse 18), but the man of God goes back with him and eats and drinks (verse 19).

At the table, the word of the LORD comes to the old prophet, and he cries out that because the man of God has defied the LORD's command, his body will not reach the tomb of his fathers (verses 20-22). On his way home ‘a lion met him on the road and killed him’ (verse 24). His body lies in the road, with the donkey and the lion standing beside it. Men passing by see it and tell the city (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The two halves of the chapter mirror each other. In both someone invites the man of God home to eat (verses 7 and 15), and in both he repeats the command he was given (verses 9 and 17). The difference is the lie of verse 18.

The title man of God was a common name for a prophet, someone sent with God's message. There were many prophets in Israel, some true and some not, and hearers had to weigh their words. The old prophet appeals to an angel, a higher authority, to overrule a clear command. The narrator says flatly that he was lying, and gives no motive. Interpreters have guessed at jealousy, a test, or a wish to share the man's honor.

The verb return and the noun way run through the story, so that the question of which road to take becomes the question of whether to obey. The irony is sharp: the lying prophet speaks the true word of judgment, and the man who defied a king's power falls to a lion.

A lion killing a traveler was a real danger in the land then. But a lion that kills and then stands still beside the body and the donkey, eating neither, is a sign that this death was a judgment, not an accident.
passages.later: The law had warned that even a prophet with a sign must not be followed away from what God has said: ‘you must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer’ (Deuteronomy 13:3).
passages.hard:
Why did the man of God die for being deceived, while the lying prophet lived?

This is one of the most troubling stories in Kings, and the text does not fully explain it. Some things are clear. The man of God had received a direct and specific command, and he had repeated it twice. The old prophet offered only a claim of a later message, which contradicted what God had already said. The story treats a prophet's obedience to his own commission as a matter of life and death, because the point of his mission was that Bethel was a place with which God's messenger could have no fellowship. By eating there, he undid the sign he had been sent to be.

The liar is not excused. He is named a liar, becomes the unwilling mouth of judgment, and ends grieving and asking to be buried beside the man he betrayed. What the story presses on its readers is that God's word must be weighed against what he has already plainly said, even when it comes from someone who claims to be a prophet.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The man of God stood firm before a king and gave way to a friendly voice. Ask which you find harder to resist, open opposition or a kind invitation that leads away from what God has said. And ask how you weigh a new word against what God has already made plain.

passages.t: A borrowed tomb, and a king who did not turn
passages.happening:
When the old prophet hears, he says, “It is the man of God who disobeyed the command of the LORD” (verse 26). He rides out and finds the body in the road, the lion and the donkey still beside it. ‘The lion had not eaten the body or mauled the donkey’ (verse 28). He brings the body back to his city, mourns him, and lays him in his own tomb, and they lament over him, “Oh, my brother!” (verse 30).

He tells his sons to bury him beside the man of God when he dies, ‘for the message that he cried out by the word of the LORD against the altar in Bethel and against all the shrines on the high places in the cities of Samaria will surely come to pass’ (verse 32).

‘Even after these events, Jeroboam did not repent of his evil ways’ (verse 33). He goes on making priests for the high places from every kind of people, anyone who wants to be one. “And this was the sin of the house of Jeroboam that led to its extermination and destruction from the face of the earth” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Burying a stranger in one's own family tomb, and asking to lie beside him, was an act of deep honor and solidarity. The old prophet who lied now confesses that the word against Bethel will stand.

The phrase the cities of Samaria is worth noticing, since the city of Samaria was not founded until Omri's reign (16:24). Many interpreters take it as the narrator's later name for the northern territory, used from the time of the book's final shaping.

The story ends where it began, with Jeroboam. He saw his hand wither and be healed, and the altar split, and still he did not turn. The verb is shuv again, the word of the road: the man of God was not to return, and the king would not return to God. Signs alone do not bring repentance; a heart must turn.
passages.later: Josiah honored the shared grave three centuries later: “Let him rest,” said Josiah. “Do not let anyone disturb his bones.” Both men's bones were left undisturbed (2 Kings 23:18). The book of Jeremiah would say the same of a later king who saw God's warnings and did not turn (Jeremiah 36:24).
passages.asks: Jeroboam saw signs with his own eyes and did not change. Ask what God has already shown you that you have not let change you. And ask what it would take for you to turn, if not what you have already seen.
